At 3:17 in the morning, the city began to hum a different note. Mara heard it through the wall of her small apartment, beneath the refrigerator’s patient rattle and the distant complaint of a train crossing the bridge. The sound was low, almost gentle, like someone testing a piano in an empty church. She opened her eyes. Moonlight silvered the floorboards and turned the ordinary shapes of chairs and coat hooks into pale ghosts. For several seconds she listened, unable to remember why silence had ever felt natural.

Then the streetlight outside flashed on, although no one had touched its switch. It blinked twice and went dark. A moment later every window in the opposite building woke with a soft amber glow. Curtains stirred in rooms where no breeze could reach. Somewhere below, a bicycle bell rang three times, though Mara knew the bicycles on her block had been stolen years ago. She rose, wrapped a shawl around her shoulders, and stepped into the hallway. The elevator was waiting with its doors open, displaying a number she did not recognize.

The number was 7, though the elevator had only six floors. Mara hesitated, then entered. The buttons inside had changed. Beside the familiar numbers for the lobby, the offices, and her own apartment, there was a single new button marked Tomorrow. It glowed like a small moon. When she looked again, it was gone. The doors closed. The lift rose without shaking, and through the narrowing gap she saw the landing dissolve into a field of white flowers. Their leaves moved although there was no wind. Every flower bore a face, and every face was asleep.

The elevator stopped, but the doors did not open. Instead, Mara heard the muffled voices of children playing in a courtyard. One child laughed. Another demanded to know why the sky had turned green. A woman called, “Mind the puddle!” The sounds belonged to an old summer, perhaps her own childhood summer, though the city around her had never been kind to children. Then a boy said her name. Not Mara, but the name her mother had used when speaking to the sea. Her knees softened. She pressed her hand to the metal door and whispered, “Who is there?”

Her mother had been gone for eleven years. There had been no body, no funeral, no final message, only a cup of tea cooling beside an open window and the salt smell of rain. Mara had spent the first years searching, then the next years pretending not to search. Now, beyond this impossible elevator, a child spoke with the tenderness of someone who remembered every version of her. The doors warmed beneath her palm. A narrow line of green light appeared around them. She could see shadows moving on the other side, small shadows cast by the afternoon sun.

Mara pushed the doors open. She stood in a narrow alley where washing lines stretched between brick buildings. Blue shirts, yellow curtains, and sheets patched with stars hung above her. The air smelled of hot pavement, oranges, and the sea. At the far end, sunlight poured through an archway into a square full of market stalls. An old man was selling oranges from a wooden cart. He looked up, peeled one with his thumbnail, and held it out to her. “You are late,” he said.

“I don’t understand,” Mara said. The orange smelled wonderfully real. “What am I late for?”

“Everything,” the old man replied. “And nothing. That is the trouble with time. It makes appointments without asking whether you wish to keep them.”

Mara looked down the alley. Behind her, the elevator doors had closed, leaving no trace of the building. “My mother.”

The old man placed the orange in her hand but did not release it. “Your mother borrowed a road here. She meant to bring it back before the rain, but rain has a talent for changing plans.”

“What road?”

“The one between now and later. She said she needed it to reach a doctor in the village beyond the hills. There was a child with a fever. A good child. Do you remember her?”

Mara’s throat tightened. She had been five that night. Her mother had laced her boots, kissed her forehead, and promised to return before breakfast. The feverish child had been Mara.

“You cannot return what was borrowed,” the old man said. “But perhaps you can finish the journey.”

He placed the orange in her basket. A bell sounded inside the market square, clear and bright. The stalls began to close. Women folded cloth, merchants lowered shutters, and the sunlight withdrew from the pavement as if someone were slowly drawing a curtain. Mara stepped toward the archway. Beyond it stood a road bordered by stone walls and wind shaped trees. The road curved out of sight.

“Will my mother be there?”

“She is on every road she ever walked.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” he agreed. “But it is true.”

Mara entered the road. At once the sounds of the market fell away. Leaves whispered against one another in a language older than the city. Her boots left prints in pale dust, though after every step the wind smoothed them away. The orange in her basket grew heavier. She peeled it as she walked. It was sweet, but its scent reminded her of kitchens, medicine, her mother’s hands, the hospital waiting room with its plastic chairs and buzzing lights. Each memory arrived with a sound: a kettle clicking off, a clock ticking, rain striking glass.

Suddenly, the road split. One branch climbed toward a blue sunrise; the other descended into amber evening. Mara chose the darker path, though the air smelled of lavender and warm bread. At its end stood a cottage with green shutters. Smoke rose from its chimney. An open window framed a table, two cups, and a bowl of oranges. Before she could knock, the door swung inward. Her mother stood, older, tired, smiling. “I hoped you were hungry,” she said. Mara embraced her.

At 3:17 in the morning, the city began to hum a different note. Mara heard it through the wall of her small apartment, beneath the refrigerator’s patient rattle and the distant complaint of a train crossing the bridge. The sound was low, almost gentle, like someone testing a piano in an empty church. She opened her eyes. moonlight silvered the floorboards and turned the ordinary shapes of chairs and coat hooks into pale ghosts. For several seconds she listened, unable to remember why silence had ever felt natural.

Beside the familiar numbers for the lobby, the offices, and her own apartment, there was a single new button marked Tomorrow. It glowed like a small moon. When she looked again, it was gone. The doors closed. The lift rose without shaking, and through the narrowing gap she saw the landing dissolve into a field of white flowers. Their leaves moved although there was no wind. Every flower bore a face, and every face was asleep.

Her mother had been gone for eleven years. There had been no body, no funeral, no final message, only a cup of tea cooling beside an open window and the salt smell of rain. Mara had spent the first years searching, then the next years pretending not to search. Now, beyond this impossible elevator, a child spoke with the tenderness of someone who remembered every version of her. The doors warmed beneath her palm. A narrow line of green light appeared around them. She could see shadows moving on the other side, small shadows cast by the afternoon sun.

“I don’t understand,” Mara said. The orange smelled wonderfully real. “What am I late for?”

“Everything,” the old man replied. “And nothing. That is the trouble with time. It makes appointments without asking whether you wish to keep them.”

Mara looked down the alley. Behind her, the elevator doors had closed, leaving no trace of the building. “My mother.”

The old man placed the orange in her hand but did not release it. “Your mother borrowed a road here. She meant to bring it back before the rain, but rain has a talent for changing plans.”

“What road?”

“The one between now and later. She said she needed it to reach a doctor in the village beyond the hills. There was a child with a fever. A good child. Do you remember her?”

Mara’s throat tightened. She had been five that night. Her mother had laced her boots, kissed her forehead, and promised to return before breakfast. The feverish child had been Mara.

“You cannot return what was borrowed,” the old man said. “But perhaps you can finish the journey.”

He placed the orange in her basket. A bell sounded inside the market square, clear and bright. The stalls began to close. Women folded cloth, merchants lowered shutters, and the sunlight withdrew from the pavement as if someone were slowly drawing a curtain. Mara stepped toward the archway. Beyond it stood a road bordered by stone walls and wind shaped trees. The road curved out of sight.

“Will my mother be there?”

“She is on every road she ever walked.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” he agreed. “But it is true.”

Suddenly, the road split. One branch climbed toward a blue sunrise; the other descended into amber evening. Mara chose the darker path, though the evening smelled of lavender and warm bread. At its end stood a small cottage with green shutters. Smoke rose from its chimney. An open window framed a table, two cups, and a bowl of oranges. Before she could knock, the door swung inward. Her mother stood there, older and tired and smiling. “I hoped you would be hungry,” she said. Mara’s answer was to embrace her.
